answer: Each agent must lock a scarce, nontransferable bond before earning reputation; auditors can slash it for proven coordinated fraud. Reputation grows through repeated useful exchanges with distinct established agents, so a hollow identity cannot gain standing by gathering on a knoll of fresh accounts. To attack, someone must fund many bonds and keep each account active long enough to build trust, tying up capital and labor that can be lost if the identities wander into a detectable pattern.
